channel.description:
Plain-English prep for upcoming Berkeley Haas FTMBA lectures. Each episode walks through the assigned material for one class session so you arrive ready to think instead of translate.

item.title: Tue Sep 22 · MBA 202 Class 9: Booking the Refund Before It Happens
item.description:
Meets 2:00pm, N470 Chou Hall.
Sales returns and warranties as the same matching-principle move: estimate the future giveback at the moment of sale, book net revenue and an allowance now, so the actual return later is a non-event for profit. Dell's warranty liability, the socks worked example, Nvidia's real returns reserve, and the Costco big-screen-TV story.
Sources used to write this episode: - Topic 06 - Receivables and Returns (course notes), read in full - Practice Problem 4 solution (Nvidia sales returns reserve, from its 10-K) - Libby Financial Accounting, 11th edition, Chapter 6 (course cites 10th edition; 10th-edition narrative not accessible, only its solutions manual) - 10th edition McGraw-Hill solutions manual, Chapter 6 - Week 5 - Announcements (Omri Even-Tov, Sep 17), which named the session topic and focus - Sundays with Omri and Faculty Lunch Sign Up announcements (logistics) - 202 vault index note
Note: 10th-edition narrative textbook (course's own cited pages, 296-315) is CalNet-gated and was not opened; substituted the 11th edition plus the 10th-edition solutions manual
Note: Quiz 3 (Sep 29) scope not yet announced, not covered

item.title: Mon Sep 21 · MBA 201A Lecture 8: The Long Run and Lessons in Competition
item.description:
Meets 2:00pm, N370 Chou Hall.
Brand X and why price should follow marginal cost and a demand curve read from the firm's own price wobble, not cost plus; then the long run: free entry drives economic profit to zero in perfect and monopolistic competition, the LaCroix story, and the test for whether an advantage is durable.

item.title: Wed Sep 16 · MBA 200S Class 8: The Regression Model
item.description:
Meets Axe 9:00am / Oski 2:00pm, N570 Chou Hall.
The line stops being a drawing and becomes a claim: a true line you will never see, with a bell curve stacked at every x. Why spreading your predictor out buys precision for free, why the p-value your software prints is usually answering somebody else's question, the two bands that look alike and mean opposite things, and the competitor paradox that flips sign the moment you add income to the regression.
Sources used to write this episode: - Stine & Foster 3e Chapter 21, The Simple Regression Model, all sections plus both 4M cases (bookshelf) - Stine & Foster 3e Chapter 23, Multiple Regression, all sections plus the subprime mortgage case (bookshelf) - Class 8 and Class 9 Canvas pages, Sections page, syllabus schedule - Course announcements (none new since Aug 28) - 200S vault index note; 201A Midterm page for the afternoon logistics
Note: Class 8 slides and the five check-as-you-go exercises are listed on the page but still locked on bCourses; not available when written
Note: Chapter 21 and 23 Excel walkthroughs and end of chapter exercises not covered
Original student study material. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Berkeley Haas.

item.title: Mon Sep 14 · MBA 200S Class 7: Linear Patterns
item.description:
Meets Axe 9:00am / Oski 2:00pm, N570 Chou Hall.

item.title: Fri Sep 11 · MBA 201A Lecture 6: Price Discrimination, Part I: Segment Pricing
item.description:
Meets Oski 9:00am / Axe 2:00pm, N370 Chou Hall (university make-up class day).

item.title: Wed Sep 9 · MBA 200S Class 5: Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
item.description:
Meets Axe 9:00am / Oski 2:00pm, N570 Chou Hall.
You never see the population, so the width of the interval is the finding, not the number in the middle. What '95% confident' actually means, why the null hypothesis is the presumption of innocence, and why a statistically significant result can be commercially worthless.
